clam.name: Clam

sections.whatItOffers: Cooked clams are an exceptional source of vitamin B12 (about 84 µg in 3 ounces, many times the 2.4 µg reference), with zinc, vitamin C and about 22 g of protein for 126 calories.
sections.howToEatIt: Steam in their shells with garlic, wine or broth, or add shucked clams to chowder, pasta and rice dishes. Discard any that stay closed after cooking.
sections.cycleRelevance: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Clams provide iron too (about 2.4 mg in this serving), in a form that is absorbed more readily than plant iron.

mussel.name: Mussel

sections.whatItOffers: Mussels are rich in vitamin B12 (about 20 µg in 3 ounces), iron (about 32% of the reference), zinc and protein (about 20 g), with some omega-3 fats.
sections.howToEatIt: Steam in a covered pot with garlic, wine or tomato until the shells open, then serve with the broth. Discard any that stay closed.
sections.cycleRelevance: Iron needs are higher for women aged 19 to 50 (18 mg a day, against 8 mg for men), partly because of menstrual blood loss (NIH ODS). Three ounces of mussels supply about 5.7 mg.

oyster.name: Oyster

sections.whatItOffers: Six cooked oysters give an exceptional amount of zinc (about 33 mg, over four times the reference), vitamin B12 and iron, for only about 43 calories.
sections.howToEatIt: Eat cooked: steam, bake or fry them, or add to stews. Raw oysters carry a food-safety risk (see the caution).
sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for oysters. Their very high zinc content means a smaller portion is plenty.

sardine.name: Sardine

sections.whatItOffers: Canned sardines, eaten with their soft bones, are rich in calcium (about 35% of the reference in one small can), vitamin B12 and vitamin D, with about 0.9 g of omega-3 fats and 23 g of protein.
sections.practicalServing: 1 small can, drained (USDA: 1 can, 3.75 oz = 92 g)
sections.howToEatIt: Mash on toast with lemon, toss into pasta or salads, or eat straight from the can with bread. The bones are soft and edible.
sections.cycleRelevance: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS); sardines eaten with their bones are one of the few non-dairy foods that give a substantial amount.

anchovies.name: Anchovies

sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for anchovies. They are mostly used for flavour, in small amounts.

trout.name: Trout

sections.whatItOffers: A cooked rainbow trout fillet is one of the richest foods in vitamin D (about 13.5 µg, 90% of the reference) and gives vitamin B12, vitamin E, about 17 g of protein and 0.6 g of omega-3 fats.
sections.howToEatIt: Pan-fry, bake whole or in fillets with lemon and herbs, or poach. The skin crisps well.
sections.cycleRelevance: Few foods contain much vitamin D. The reference for women 19 to 50 is 15 µg a day (NIH ODS), and a trout fillet supplies about 90% of it.

canned-salmon.name: Canned salmon

sections.whatItOffers: Canned pink salmon, eaten with its soft bones, gives vitamin B12, vitamin D (about 82% of the reference), calcium (about 24%) and 0.9 g of omega-3 fats, with about 20 g of protein in 3 ounces.
sections.howToEatIt: Flake into salads, sandwiches, fish cakes and pasta, or mix with yoghurt and herbs. The soft bones can be mashed in.
sections.cycleRelevance: Calcium needs are 1,000 mg a day, and vitamin D 15 µg a day, for women aged 19 to 50 (NIH ODS). Canned salmon with the bones supplies a good share of both.

canned-tuna.name: Canned tuna

sections.whatItOffers: Canned light tuna in water is a lean, convenient protein: 3 ounces give about 16.5 g of protein and 90% of the vitamin B12 reference for 73 calories. It has far less omega-3 fat than oily fish.
sections.howToEatIt: Mix with yoghurt or mayonnaise for sandwiches, toss into pasta and salads, or bake into fish cakes.
sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for tuna. FDA and EPA list canned light tuna as a "Best Choice" for mercury; albacore (white) tuna is a "Good Choice".

mackerel.name: Mackerel

sections.cycleRelevance: No cycle-phase claim is made for mackerel. FDA and EPA list Atlantic mackerel as a "Best Choice" for mercury, but not king mackerel.
